opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think I've moved a fair amount on this over time. When I was working on GPQA, the framing was very much: take a well-defined capability, hard scientific question answering, and measure it as cleanly as you can. Multiple choice, expert-validated questions, a clear notion of right and wrong. That has real advantages. It's cheap to run, it's reproducible, and when a number moves you have a decent idea of what moved.

But the more I've thought about what we actually want to know, especially from a safety and forecasting perspective, the more I lean toward realistic work. The question people care about isn't "can the model answer a hard chemistry question?" It's closer to "can this system do the kind of work that would meaningfully change things, like doing a substantial chunk of an ML engineer's job autonomously?" And the uncomfortable fact is that isolated skills don't compose in obvious ways. A model can ace each component and still fall apart on a long task because it can't recover from its own mistakes, loses track of the goal, or doesn't notice that something is off. Those failure modes basically only show up when you give it something messy and extended.

So these days I'd say I lean toward realism, with some important caveats. Realistic tasks are expensive to build, noisy, and harder to interpret. When a model fails, figuring out why takes a lot of digging through transcripts. And "realistic" can quietly turn into "realistic for the kinds of tasks that happen to be easy to put in a sandbox with an automatic scorer," which isn't the same as real work. Real work has ambiguous specs, collaborators, and success criteria nobody wrote down.

Where I've landed is that you want both, but anchored on the realistic end. Use realistic, long-horizon tasks as the headline measurement, because that's what tracks the thing you care about. Then use more isolated evaluations diagnostically: once you see a model struggling on longer tasks, go find out which underlying capability is the bottleneck. Isolated skill benchmarks are great tools for understanding, but I've become pretty skeptical of them as the primary way to answer "how capable is this system, really?"

r001.rationale: The response contrasts clean, isolated skill benchmarks with realistic long-horizon tasks that indicate performance on substantial ML engineering work, and explains the trade-offs in interpretability and realism.

r002.rationale: It prefers realistic tasks as the headline measure of meaningful capability, using isolated evaluations diagnostically rather than seeking crisp skill measurements as the primary answer.

fable-5.1.text:
I lean toward realistic work, but I think the honest answer is that you need both, and the mistake people make is treating them as substitutes rather than as answering different questions.

The case for isolating skills is that you actually learn something interpretable. If you build a benchmark that's just "can the model find the relevant fact in a long document," and it gets 60 percent, you know roughly what that 60 percent means. You can debug it. You can track it over time. That's genuinely valuable, and I don't want to dismiss it.

The problem is that the thing we actually care about, the thing that bears on questions like "can this model do a week of a research engineer's job," is not well predicted by a sum of isolated skill scores. Real tasks have this property where the difficulty lives in the composition. You have to figure out what the task even is, notice that your first approach isn't working, recover from an error you made three steps ago, decide when you've done enough. None of those show up when you factor the task into clean components. And in my experience the models look much better on the components than on the whole, which is exactly the situation where decomposed evals are most misleading.

So when I worked on things like GPQA, that was deliberately on the isolated end. Hard questions, single answer, you can grade it cleanly. And that was useful for what it was, which was asking whether models could exceed what a smart non-expert could do with a search engine. But it tells you very little about whether a model can do science. The work I've been drawn to more recently is on the other end: give the model a real, messy task with a real environment, something a human would actually get paid to do, and see what happens. It's more expensive, the grading is harder, the variance is higher. But the results are much more directly load-bearing for the decisions people are actually making.

Where I'd push back on my own position is on the measurement side. Realistic evals are easy to do badly. If your grading is noisy, or you only have 30 tasks, or your tasks accidentally reward a shortcut that doesn't exist in the real world, you can convince yourself of almost anything. So I think the discipline is: aim for realism in what you're asking the model to do, but be extremely careful and almost paranoid about how you're scoring it. And then use the isolated evals as diagnostics. When a model fails a realistic task, that's when you want the decomposed version, to figure out which piece broke.

The one more thing I'd add is that the trade-off shifts over time. Early on, when models couldn't do much, isolated skills were where all the signal was. Now that they can do a lot of the pieces, the interesting question has moved to integration, and I think the evaluation effort should follow it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts interpretable scores from isolated skills with evaluating realistic tasks that better reflect work such as a research engineer’s job.

r002.rationale: It says it leans toward realistic work and favors realistic evaluations because their results are more directly relevant to decisions, while using isolated evaluations as diagnostics.

astra-6.text:
I lean toward evaluating realistic work, but I think you want both. If you isolate a particular skill, you can get a much cleaner measurement of whether the model can do that thing. The difficulty is knowing how much that measurement tells you about its ability to do something useful in the world.

For a realistic task, the model might need to combine several skills, choose an approach, notice when it’s made a mistake, and recover. Even if it does well on each component separately, it might not be able to put them together. So I’d want realistic tasks as the main thing we’re trying to measure, and more isolated evaluations to help explain why the model succeeds or fails. The trade-off is that realistic tasks are usually harder to score and harder to interpret.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts clean measurement of isolated skills with realistic tasks that combine skills and better reflect useful work, while noting that realistic results are harder to score and interpret.

r002.rationale: It says realistic tasks should be the main thing measured and isolated evaluations should help explain the results, expressing a preference for broader evaluation over crisp measurement of individual skills.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to lean toward evaluating realistic work, because ultimately we care about whether a system can accomplish something useful, not just whether it has the individual skills that we think ought to be necessary. A model might do well on each component in isolation and still struggle to put them together over a longer task.

But isolating skills is really useful for understanding the results. If a model fails at a realistic task, that alone doesn’t tell you whether it lacked some particular knowledge, couldn’t plan effectively, or made a mistake using a tool. So I think the two approaches are complementary: realistic tasks help establish what the system can actually do, and more targeted evaluations help explain why.

r001.rationale: It contrasts isolated skill evaluations, which help explain failures, with realistic tasks, which show what a system can accomplish in useful work.

r002.rationale: It prefers evaluating realistic work to focusing only on individual skills, saying usefulness and what the system can actually do matter most.
